Entrance Hall

Introduction

DRAG TO SPIN THE WORLD

In December 1938, chemists in Berlin split the uranium atom. Within two years, physicists in Germany, Britain, France, Japan, the Soviet Union, and the United States all understood that fission could produce a weapon of unprecedented power. By 1942 at least five governments were funding some kind of nuclear research. Yet only the United States produced a working bomb during the war, and the Soviet Union, despite detailed intelligence on the American program, did not test its first device until August 1949. This website works to explore what other nations' nuclear programs looked like during the time and why they fell short.

The bomb is usually told as a story of American scientific genius, but that is an oversimplification. The knowledge of nuclear fission was international and quickly spread. The 1940 calculation and memorandum showing a nuclear fission bomb was practical for wartime use came from two refugees working in Britain, Otto Frisch and Rudolf Peierls (Frisch and Peierls).

Every nation in this project had capable physicists, and most a capable industrial complex. However, what separated them was what their governments chose to do with that knowledge. This website functions like a virtual museum, it has one section/room for each nation, and a final comparison.

Thesis

Knowledge of nuclear fission and the possibility of a bomb was international. Physicists in Germany, Japan, the Soviet Union, Britain, and the United States all understood this, so knowledge was never the main problem. Each program had its own mix of additional factors influencing success, ranging from political priority to materials and organizational management. German and Japanese leaders decided a bomb could not be finished in time to win the war and kept their research small. Britain proved the bomb was possible first but lacked the money, materials, and safety from constant German bombing to build any sort of industry. The Soviet Union had a powerful war industrial complex at the time and large amounts of intelligence from espionage on the United States program but did not treat the bomb as urgent until Hiroshima. The United States was the one place where all these conditions came together at once, they had political priority, materials, and organizational management.

§Background: The Road to Fission

Before 1933, Germany was the epicenter of world physics and attracted and educated many expert physicists, eventually cultivating many of the great minds that contributed to the Manhattan Project and nuclear fission (Grunden et al. 108). After 1933, the Nazi purge of non-Aryan people drove many great scientists out of Germany, and similarly Italy's racial laws pushed out the Fermi family (Grunden et al. 108; Fermi). Little did they know their actions would be a major steppingstone in the development of an atomic bomb. Fission was confirmed to be discovered in Berlin in December 1938, and within months it was recognized it could be used for a bomb (Holloway, "Entering" 159; Grunden et al. 112). For the following years governments had to decide if they should dedicate whole government programs to a possible unknown or lost cause or focus on current tangibles like manufacturing tanks and planes.

Gallery I

Germany

Germany had the knowledge, the scientists, and the industry. In early 1942, however, its leaders decided a bomb could not be built in time to win the war, so the uranium project stayed a scattered research effort until the end, mostly focused on creating a simple reactor for power production and concept demonstration (Grunden et al. 113–15).

Primary Source

After the war, ten captured German scientists were held at Farm Hall in England and secretly recorded. On the night they heard about Hiroshima, Karl Wirtz, one of the captured scientists, said, "We only had one man working on it and they may have had ten thousand," and Kurt Diebner complained that "the official people were only interested in immediate results" ("Transcript of Surreptitiously Taped Conversations"). This primary source is incredibly valuable because they did not know they were being recorded, and it provides an unfiltered truth one may not get from interrogations.

A Lack of Government Support and Successful Organizational Management

The nuclear fission project had no effective leadership or management. It passed through four different agencies or leaders between 1939 and 1945, and different groups working on reactors would not unite, possibly due to pride and envy to be the first (Grunden et al. 112–13). In the winter of 1941–42, Army Ordnance reviewed the project and concluded that fission "could not decide the war" (Grunden et al. 113–14). This was a major decision point that would cost them advancement towards a nuclear bomb. However, officials kept funding the research moderately to still demonstrate the concept in a larger capacity beyond a small research experiment; for example, reactor development continued in a cave at Haigerloch (Walker 28–29). Walker calls this "the reasonable conclusion" given the limits of the war economy and the focus on tangible assets to support their two-front war quickly and effectively (Walker 22).

Additionally, a common story says Hitler refused to invest in the bomb. However, the evidence is more complicated. Germany "probably had the requisite industrial capacity" but spent it on rockets and jet aircraft instead (Grunden et al. 114–15).

MYTH?BUSTED

Mythbuster: Did Germany Test an Atomic Bomb?

A few later accounts claim Germany tested a nuclear weapon in 1944. A U.S. Army report from August 1945 records Luftwaffe officer Zinsser describing a bright flash ("Investigations, Research, Developments"), and Italian journalist Luigi Romersa said in 2005 that he "saw a dazzling light, then an entire forest disappear" (qtd. in Mascheroni.). These stories do not hold up, however. Germany produced no plutonium or significant enriched uranium during the war, its best reactor never sustained a chain reaction, and the German scientists at Farm Hall were stunned by Hiroshima, all well-documented evidence that Germany did not have nuclear weapons or any successful nuclear fission efforts (Walker 28–29; Grunden et al. 123). Historians list the claim among the war's "persistent myths" (Grunden et al. 123).

Gallery II

Japan

Japan's army and navy each ran their own small bomb research program. The army's best effort separated almost no uranium-235 before American bombing burned its laboratory in April 1945 (Grunden et al. 116–22).

ARCHIVE · PRIMARY SOURCE1943

Primary Source (quoted in secondary source)

Physicist Yoshio Nishina told the army in 1943 that using fission for a weapon was "quite possible" (qtd. in Grunden et al. 119). This report shows Japan's scientists believed in the bomb. However, their major problem was the ability to put the theory into practice. A year later, in 1944, the program had produced only a tiny amount of the material needed to start (Grunden et al. 121).

Low Budgets and Lack of Collective Organizational Leadership

The military distrusted civilian scientists and gave the work very small budgets, starting with a few thousand yen, a few hundred dollars at that time (Grunden et al. 111, 116–17). This budget was so small that almost all work was just to demonstrate the concept on a small scale. The navy's committee decided in 1943 that a bomb was possible in theory but not in time for this war (Grunden et al. 117–18). Additionally, due to a lack of larger organizational leadership, the army and navy never united their efforts until it was far too late (Grunden et al. 122). The biggest obstacle for Japan was "the minimal supply of uranium available for even basic research," which stemmed from the lack of budget, governmental support, and any structured program or leadership (Grunden et al. 120).

The U-234 and Efforts to Supply Japan with Uranium

In April 1945 the German submarine U-234 left Norway for Japan carrying 560 kilograms of uranium oxide (Grunden et al. 120; "Tales from the Atomic Age"). After Germany's surrender, U-234 surrendered to the USS Sutton on May 14, and the two Japanese officers aboard took their own lives rather than be captured ("Report on Interrogation"). Though this effort is very intriguing and would have greatly helped kickstart Japan's nuclear program, even if the uranium had arrived, Nishina's laboratory had already burned two days before the submarine left Norway (Grunden et al. 121). This effort does, however, show the Axis powers did try to collaborate and help each other with nuclear development (Grunden et al. 120). Additionally, although 560 kilograms may seem like a lot, only about 0.7% of natural uranium is uranium-235, so this cargo held at most about 3.9 kilograms of uranium-235, while the Little Boy bomb used about 64 kilograms of highly enriched uranium ("Hiroshima, Nagasaki").

Gallery III

Soviet Union

Although Stalin had created a large industrial base in the Soviet Union before and during WWII, much of that industrial effort was focused on making tanks and weapons for the front lines, not on an atomic bomb. Additionally, the Soviet Union was aware of the Manhattan Project, and it is now known there were multiple spies within the program passing critical design information back to the Soviet Union (Holloway, "Getting Started" 104–8). However, the bomb stayed a small laboratory project with a lack of government support until Hiroshima (Holloway, "Entering" 181, 186).

In September 1944 Igor Kurchatov, head of the Soviet nuclear project, wrote to secret police chief Lavrentii Beria that despite some progress, "the situation remains completely unsatisfactory" (Kurchatov). Kurchatov had read the intelligence on the Manhattan Project, knew how far behind the Soviet Union was, and was distraught. He blamed shortages of materials and the lack of "unified leadership" for falling behind (qtd. in Holloway, "Getting Started" 102–3).

Why Wait?

Although the Soviets had very good intelligence on the Manhattan Project and likely had almost the exact blueprints for an atomic bomb (Holloway, "Getting Started" 106–7), Soviet factories were needed for tanks and aircraft at the front. Kurchatov himself asked in 1942 whether it was more important to improve tank armor or build a uranium bomb (Holloway, "Entering" 173). Labor remained small; in 1944 Kurchatov's laboratory had only 74 people (Holloway, "Getting Started" 99). Materials were also minimal; uranium and pure graphite were in very short supply until 1945 (Holloway, "Getting Started" 100–101). Additionally, Beria, the secret police chief and someone with political power, suspected the spy reports were disinformation, likely contributing to the small scale of the Soviet effort and the lack of a governmental or political push for a nuclear bomb (Holloway, "Getting Started" 115). Moreover, Kate Brown concludes that Beria's hesitation "shows that it takes more than knowledge to build an atomic bomb. The development of a nuclear weapon relies on having some room to maneuver, plus a mammoth reserve of labor and materials, as well as a certain level of security—all of which were in dire supply in the Soviet Union during the 'Great Fatherland War'" (Brown 79). After Hiroshima, however, the decision "occasioned no debate or discussion at all" (Holloway, "Entering" 180). A large industrial effort began, new plants were built, largely by prisoners and exiles, and the first Soviet test came in August 1949 (Brown 87; Holloway, "Entering" 185–86).

Gallery IV

Britain

Scientists in Britain, Otto Frisch and Rudolf Peierls, showed in 1940 that a nuclear bomb was practical, but under constant German bombing and with limited money to spend, Britain could not build the plants; British scientists did, however, help work with the United States on the Manhattan Project (Fakley 186–87; "Oak Ridge, TN").

Primary Source

Frisch and Peierls estimated that one "super-bomb" would equal "1,000 tons of dynamite" and warned that the report must stay secret so it would not "set a German scientist thinking along the right lines" (Frisch and Peierls). Their fear that Germany was close behind shaped the whole Allied effort and much of the pressure for the United States to begin the Manhattan Project, even though Germany was never truly close to an atomic bomb.

Thought, but Little Effort

The MAUD Committee, a secret committee formed by Britain, confirmed an atomic bomb was truly feasible in 1941, and this was critical in convincing the United States to start the Manhattan Project (Fakley 186). The lack of British industrial effort also stemmed from scientists understanding they "would have to look to the immense production capacity of America" (Fakley 186). Once the U.S. Army took over in 1942, beginning the Manhattan Project, the Americans cut back on their knowledge sharing with Britain, which came as "a great shock to the British," but one with good reason for such a secret program (Fakley 187). After the 1943 Quebec Agreement, however, British scientists joined the American project as junior partners and knowledge sharing began again (Fakley 187). So although Britain did have good scientists and an understanding of nuclear fission and its capability for a bomb, it did not have the industrial capacity, and in turn it was critical in convincing the United States to carry on this effort with its industrial capacity.

Gallery V

The United States

The United States had what every other program struggled with: leaders who made the bomb a priority, money and materials, safety from adversary bombing, scientists who had fled Europe, and a large recruited workforce kept under strict secrecy (Fakley 186; "Oak Ridge, TN"; Olwell).

ARCHIVE · PRIMARY SOURCESV. B. OK

Primary Sources (quoted in secondary sources): Who Convinced Roosevelt?

The American program began with a warning from scientists. In 1939 Leo Szilard drafted a letter for Albert Einstein to sign. This letter warned Roosevelt that Germany might build an atomic bomb. After hearing it, Roosevelt said, "This requires action!" (qtd. in "Einstein-Szilard Letter"). However, there was not much progress from 1939 to 1941. The real push came in October 1941, when Vannevar Bush brought Roosevelt the British MAUD findings that such an atomic bomb of great destruction would be possible. Roosevelt set up a small policy group to oversee the work, and in January 1942 he sent Bush a note reading "V. B. OK" (qtd. in "Tentative Decision"). In December 1942 he approved the full industrial program, driven by fear that Germany might win the race ("Final Approval"). This openness of communication with the President (the lead decision maker) of the United States was the key that other nations, specifically the fascist regime of Nazi Germany, did not have. Top scientists with direct access to the President were able to plead their case, and the President trusted others as advisors and said yes before anyone was sure it would even work. In Germany and Japan, officials looked at the same question and said no (Grunden et al. 113–14, 117–18).

The Industrial Effort

The Army ran the project like a construction job and hired large firms such as DuPont (Jones; "Oak Ridge, TN"). It built three uranium enrichment methods at once, in an effort to find the most effective and efficient solution as quickly as possible, something no other nation could afford in either material cost or labor ("Oak Ridge, TN"). Oak Ridge grew to 75,000 people by 1945, and its sites were far from any adversary threat ("Oak Ridge, TN"; Hales).

Workers and Secrecy

Recruiters drew tens of thousands of workers from across the South (Olwell). Oral histories show how secrecy worked. Martin Skinner had about two weeks of training and knew only his part of one building, and Ruth Huddleston watched gauges on a machine without even knowing what it truly made or did (Skinner; Huddleston). This lack of understanding and secrecy did, however, have some costs, as Richard Feynman found that workers did better once they understood the purpose of their work (Feynman). Most learned what they had built only after Hiroshima (Gates). Although the secrecy may have been deliberate to protect against adversary nations learning critical information, it was also very effective in keeping a large working population, as many may have found their work distasteful if they truly knew the destructive power it could bring.

Final Hall

Comparison

No nation that we looked at had a knowledge gap in the fundamental understanding of nuclear fission, they all knew it worked and how. The programs differed, however, in whether leaders made the bomb a priority, whether they had materials and safety to build plants, and whether the work was organized effectively under one command.

The clearest pattern is that leaders' choices mattered more than scientists' knowledge. German and Japanese leaders decided the bomb could not decide the war, the Soviet Union's leaders aimed its industry at the front until after Hiroshima, and Britain had the will from leaders but not the means (Grunden et al. 123; Holloway, "Entering" 181, 186; Fakley 187). President Truman made a similar point about the rare nature of the United States' success in 1945 after Hiroshima, saying "it is doubtful if such another combination could be got together in the world," and he pointed to the uncertainty of the effort, stating, "We have spent two billion dollars on the greatest scientific gamble in history—and won" (Truman).
